Like, again, I'm in no way trying to be mean here--this deck clearly
looks like it is doing something really clever (if really obscure).
And it won a tournament, so clearly it worked against a presumably
average field of decks. But still. I'm totally not seeing at all what
it is doing to do something other than maybe get out a bunch of
allies, call Autarkis Persecution, gain a bunch of pool, give a bunch
of pool to everyone else, beat some folks up with Rock Cats (assuming
they have no combat defense whatsoever) and then eventually get Mata
Hari out and see her get killed for being Red List.

Could someone who was near this deck enlighten us?

> Crypt [(17 vampires, average capacity: 2)

> 1x      Shawnda Dorrit  CEL obt pot pre         6       Brujah antitribu:4      priscus

Ok. If you can get out both Mata and Shawnda, you can theoretically
have 5 votes. Which makes passing the Autarkis easier. But you are
unlikely to draw Mata or Shawnda till you play a whole bunch of
Tupdogs. Which is costing pool and Tupdogs can't take D actions. So
you spend a bunch or pool and turns getting out Tupdogs who maybe get
some Rock Cats as you fish for Mata Hari. And then get ousted?

> Library (60 cards)
> -------------------
> Master (10)

> 1x      Jake Washington (Hunter)
> 3x      Memories of Mortality

being ousted.

Ok. Lots of allies. So you get out lots of allies. Including Rock Cat,
who is really good at killing weenie vampires. But not real good
against bigger vampires with things like manuevers or guns. Or
Potence. And they cost 4 pool. And can't bleed. But in any case, you
get out a lot of allies and call Autarkis. Which gives you a bunch of
pool. To get more allies. That can't bleed much. And gives out more
pool to your prey, which you can't really take away from your prey.

> Event (3)
> 1x      Dragonbound
> 2x      Unmasking, The

Unmasking is good. Gives your allies +1 intercept. But it stops there.
Dragonbound is good. If your prey has a lot of little vampires in
torpor from getting beat up by Rock Cats.

> Political Action (8)
> 7x      Autarkis Persecution
> 1x      Mark of the Damned

Ok. The Autarkis is key, certainly. But it gives you pool, gives your
prey pool, gives your predator pool, and makes sure folks never get
ousted. Especially your prey? And the Mark of the Damned is likely to
make you lose a lot of pool (due to the burned Tupdogs) and not make
anyone else lose much pool.

> Reaction (4)
> 4x      Bloodstorm of Chorazin

Reasonable. If Mata Hari could reliably block anyone.

> Retainer (1)
> 1x      D'habi Revenant

Good.

> Combat (7)
> 3x      Disarm
> 4x      Immortal Grapple

Good for Rock Cat, sure. Unless someone Manuevers to long with a Gun
or something.

Like, again, really, I'm not trying to be mean or slag the deck or
anything. It looks clearly very well thought out. And looks like it
could do well in a really specific, weird environment (where everyone
else is, say, playing lots of little weenie vampires with no combat
defense at all, and not a ton of bleed. And not a ton of intercept.
And no combat offense.) It is also possible that there is a rules/card
text misunderstanding somewhere that everyone missed out on that could
use some illumination.

Anyone?

I'm guessing that's all the Tupdogs really need to do. The Rock Cats

worse than wasting a bunch of combat cards on a crappy ally for a
combat deck - and combat decks aren't that popular to begin with.

Small deck, lots of things that can get out of your hand quickly. If
someone blocks, so what, you can pull out another and another, until
they can't.

As I said, I really think the only way a deck like this could win is
either through king-making, or by successively backousting everyone on
the table, one at a time, using Waste Management Operation and Mark of
the Damned, and keeping everyone else afloat by autarkis persecution
until you get through to them. That way everyone ends up with 1VP and
you end up with 2. Still, like you said, with very little stealth,
it's surprising nobody was there with a smattering of intercept to
stop the deck flat.

Maybe not a GW, but good enough to get you into the finals, and good
enough to win the tournament at the end. I've seen some pretty crummy
last-seed decks win tournaments in the past, because all the other big
bad decks proceeded to knock the snot out of each other and pave the
way for others to take a couple of VP's and win.

There are many more situations where first turn x3 Tupdog, second turn
x3 Rock Cat is a problem than just when playing zero combat defense
and tiny vampires.

S:CE is likely to run out against three rushes a turn, nevermind IG.
Fortitude is in a lot more trouble due to the Cat's press. How many
decks just beat Rock Cat in combat? Animalism, sure. If you have the
Concealed .44 as soon as you bring out a vamp, sure. Others too, but
not so many.

Even a trade isn't productive - in the early game, trading a RC for a
vampire should be in favor of this deck.

That being said, if you know the deck, there are some things I'd
consider early in the game even when not facing x3 Cats before
bringing out a vamp.

First, the general strategy would be to attack the player's pool.
Down low enough and the pool cost of Tupdog/Cat becomes prohibitive.
Of course, this is where Autarkis comes in; given a Cheetah start, the
pool gain can go off before there's opposition or the Cats can take
out voters first, which provides the fuel to flood the table with more
Cats.

Second, bring out more than one minion at once with the idea that one
of them can get through for pool damage.

Third, coordinate with the player on the other side. If the predator
of the deck, then bringing out minions right behind the deck's prey
puts a lot of targets in play, though the deck would still likely try
to maim the predator first. If the prey, plan on rescuing the deck's
predator to put pressure on it. Even the deck's grandpredator may
like the idea of its prey getting beaten down repeatedly before either
ousting the deck or failing to.

It would be interesting to know how much game there is without a
strong start, but the potential out of the gate does seem to be an
important part that is getting missed. Then, many players aren't
mentally prepared for every deck, so the potential for making a
mistake against this one seems much higher than normal. Most of this
thread is about not understanding the deck, which should be evidence
enough of this angle to it.

city with 2 very powerful trick decks. After he played them and took

last past it's first game here, cos once everyone saw them being
played, and figured out how they worked, they wouldn't get going

ground - and it wasn't revenge (no table gang-up or anything), just

round, and once one or two essential cogs were stopped, the whole deck
fell apart. (In context - one of the decks was a multi-rush star-deck,

in playing the table.

Thanks. The point I was trying to make is that you would nullify your
prey pretty quickly. Even with this mistake, it still doesn't debunk
my argument though. Perhaps my judgement comes from our playgroup
here, but generally, a deck like this, that pulls out hordes of
minions, will get a whole lot of table hate here, especially since the
deck is also doing a whole lot of stuff. The threat appears too
immediate and obvious, even if it was unfounded. That, combined with
the ease at which it can completely and utterly fall apart when the
table does turn against you, is what makes me think the person got
more lucky than anything else.

However, I do think that the deck archetype (Tup Dogs and Rock Cats)
is quite clever, just this particular version of it seems particularly
fragile. For me, I'd definitely include a bit more of the lynch-pin
cards (another Dragonbound for starters) and some fail-safe options
(like IR Goggles and/or maneuvers).

Again, I find it hard to imagine a tournament with 21 players and 3/4
rounds of play that somebody on my table would not have some style of
deck that could completely tear this specific deck apart, and would
consider myself extremely lucky if I didn't face one of these decks.
Although, knowing my luck, I'd probably have one as my prey and
another as my predator in at least one of the rounds.
